The study assumes a scenario where OTEC systems are integrated into new facilities during the design phase, as retrofitting existing facilities is deemed cost-prohibitive. Existing offshore oil and gas facilities in the Gulf of America (GOA) are considered hypothetical scenarios due to their variable service life and potential unsuitability for OTEC integration. Stakeholders must consider location-specific factors, such as regulatory restrictions and economic feasibility, when making decisions about OTEC integration. The real Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) calculations provide a theoretical view of OTEC’s potential, although there remains limited operational experience or high uncertainty with both capital and operation and maintenance cost data with OTEC globally. Key insights from the study include the need for OTEC systems to have key equipment within 30 feet of the sea-water surface for peak efficiency. The seasonal variation in surface water temperatures in the GOA poses a challenge for large-scale OTEC deployment, yet the region’s marine resources still make it a promising candidate for OTEC. Water depths beyond 1,000 meters do not significantly enhance temperature differentials. The current largest commercially available cold-water intake pipe limits power availability at a single location, highlighting the need for research into larger and more efficient OTEC components. iv OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 Remaining uncertainties include the need for improved local temperature data, a hydrodynamic study of the add-on concept, and the development of self-cleaning heat exchangers to reduce costs. While this study focused on new facilities, the potential for retrofitting existing or retired facilities for OTEC integration also warrants further exploration. v OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 1 Introduction The United States is faced with increasing demand for energy security while simultaneously addressing the environmental impacts of energy production. Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) emerges as a promising technology in this context, offering the potential to harness the vast thermal energy stored in the world's oceans. OTEC is capable of synergizing with offshore oil and gas operations to both offset a facility’s power demand as well as power emerging demands, such as potentially monitoring plugged and abandoned offshore wells for unintended methane emissions or monitoring subsea geologic carbon storage. This report focuses on the feasibility and potential benefits of collocating OTEC systems with offshore oil and gas facilities, particularly in the Gulf of America (GOA), to meet the power demands of these installations while contributing to a reduction in GHG emissions. This report is part of a larger study titled Application of Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) Systems for Powering Safety Monitoring Systems of Offshore Oil and Gas Operations. The reports produced in the course of this study were broken up into three volumes.
